While that work is taking place, the team can review the diagrams in the meeting room and prepare questions about the maintenance schedule. The site manager will explain which parts of the system remain in service during the check and which parts have been isolated. A red notice will remain on the chamber door, and the key will stay with the safety officer rather than being passed between members of the visiting group. The organizer has arranged a separate route to the viewing area so that the group can observe the external controls without crossing the barrier. That route must remain clear of delivery carts throughout the morning. After the check, the officer will decide whether the chamber can be opened for the supervised visit described in the schedule. The decision will be written down along with the time at which the check was completed. The visitors will then receive a short briefing that distinguishes the areas they may enter from the equipment they may only observe. The organizer will keep a list of everyone who has attended that briefing and will tell late arrivals where they must wait. The present instruction concerns the period before the pressure check is complete; it should not be rewritten as an obligation to inspect the chamber during that period. The team has been told that the entire visit may be postponed if the required conditions cannot be met.

Ask what main claim these circumstances qualify, rather than inventing one or deleting a conjunction to select an intended relationship. Mentioning expressions of relief is not itself using an interjection, but the incomplete message precludes a missing-target verdict here. Standalone reactions can be valid; this input is instead an unfinished linked proposition in sentence mode. The supplied excerpts support the fragment analysis, not a comprehensive judgment about interjection usage or language variation.

acceptedCorrectionExamples: At the public meeting, the reporter asked where the donated maps came from, because the exhibition label named the donor but gave no account of the collection's earlier history. The question concerned the maps' origin, not the location of a delivery van or the address of the museum. Several residents had noticed pencil notes in the margins and wanted to know whether those notes had been made by a surveyor, a teacher, or a later owner. The curator explained that the museum had not yet identified every mark and would keep its description provisional until the records had been checked. She showed the audience a photograph of the box in which the maps had arrived, taking care to hide the address on the shipping label. The reporter wrote down the date of the donation and the reference number that would allow readers to find the public catalogue entry. He did not present the possible explanations as established facts. During the discussion, another visitor mentioned a local society that had once used similar paper for its field notes. That observation gave the curator a useful lead, but it did not prove that the society had owned these particular maps. A volunteer offered to search the society's published reports while the museum examined the condition of the paper. The group agreed that any account of the maps' history should distinguish direct documentation from reasonable guesses. The reporter planned a short article about that process rather than a dramatic story based on a single unverified remark. Before leaving, he checked the spelling of the donor's name against the version already published in the catalogue. The museum would not publish a revised description until it could explain which records supported each new statement. In the meantime, the existing label would remain beside the display, accompanied by a note saying that further research was in progress. Visitors were invited to share relevant public records through the museum's usual enquiry form.

acceptedCorrectionExamples: The coordinator plans to deliver the revised route map to every guide tomorrow morning, before the first visitors reach the temporary entrance. The map shows a short diversion around the part of the courtyard where the drainage work is still in progress. It also marks the doorway that can be used by people who cannot manage the steps beside the ticket office. During the trial walk, two guides noticed that the signs at the far end of the diversion were difficult to see when a delivery vehicle was parked nearby. The coordinator asked the maintenance team to move those signs onto fixed supports rather than attach them to the temporary fence. A copy of the revised map will be kept at the entrance so that staff can answer questions without relying on a version stored on someone's telephone. The guides will have a short meeting before the gates open to compare the map with the route as it appears on the ground. If any barrier has been moved overnight, they will report the change before leading a group through the courtyard. The organizer wants visitors to receive the same basic information regardless of which guide they happen to ask. That does not mean the guides must repeat an identical speech; it means that the directions, restrictions, and access arrangements should be consistent. The office will record the version number printed in the corner of the map and will remove the older copies from the usual distribution points. Staff should not throw away the signed inspection record that explains why the diversion was introduced. That record is part of the account of the building work, whereas the loose maps are practical instructions for the current visit. The coordinator will check that distinction during the morning meeting. Once the work in the courtyard is finished, the route can be reviewed again, but tomorrow's visitors still need a clear and accurate description of the temporary arrangement.
